start_here:
Xinhua, CGTN, China Daily, Global Times, People's Daily and China News Service are owned and run by the Chinese state. Their job is to represent China's government to the world, not to report on it independently. Their text still ends up in ordinary newsrooms abroad. It arrives through wire subscriptions, where an outlet pays for a feed of Xinhua stories and can publish them as its own copy; through content-sharing agreements between national news agencies and Xinhua or China Media Group; through paid supplements and sponsored sections placed inside mainstream papers; and through signed opinion pieces written by Chinese ambassadors and embassy staff. None of this is unusual on its own. Wire services from many countries work the same way, and running a wire story can be an ordinary, disclosed part of how a newsroom fills space on a given day.

The problem is when readers cannot tell where the words came from. If a Chinese state agency's copy runs without a credit, or a local reporter repeats an official Chinese claim without checking it, a reader experiences it as independent local journalism, when it is not.

This tracker counts. It reads the full text of articles from a fixed list of outlets, every day, and records how often Chinese state text appears without substantive change and how often local reporters pass on official Chinese claims unchecked. It does not judge why any single outlet ran a story, and it does not claim a given placement was hidden or sinister. Running a wire story can be routine. The counting is the whole claim; nothing here is a verdict on intent.

state_origin.label: State origin
state_origin.definition: Text written by an arm of the Chinese state, or commissioned by one, and published without substantive editorial change: Xinhua wire stories, CGTN release copy, China Daily and Global Times syndicated pieces, sponsored placements commissioned by Chinese state entities (even when the outlet's own branded content studio wrote them), and opinion columns signed by Chinese diplomats. The words are the state's, written by it or to its order, and the outlet that ran them did not substantively change them. Deciding to run a piece is not a change.

unchecked_state_sourcing.label: Unchecked state sourcing
unchecked_state_sourcing.definition: An article written by the local newsroom's own staff, not copied from a Chinese source, whose main point is a factual claim from an official Chinese source (a ministry spokesperson, an embassy, or Xinhua), such as a figure or an account of what happened, repeated as fact without any independent check. Reporting what Beijing says it wants, warns, threatens or denies does not count: that is reporting a stated position, and it is independent journalism even when nobody else is quoted. This is the harder call, so an AI model makes it once, following the author's written codebook, rather than a fixed rule. The counts are provisional until people check that judgement: the owner and two research assistants hand code a fixed random sample, about 200 articles in each language with at least 300 model-labelled articles, stratified by language and, within each language, by the model's category, and the counts are published only if their agreement with the model reaches a Cohen's kappa of 0.6. An earlier check, in which the same model re-judged a sample of its own past calls under earlier instructions, can show only whether its judgement is stable, not whether it is right, and is kept as history.

official_chinese_sourcing_verification_p.label: Official Chinese sourcing, verification pending
official_chinese_sourcing_verification_p.definition: Articles flagged for the model: official Chinese sourcing (a citation of Xinhua, an embassy, or a foreign ministry spokesperson, say), a weak signature, or a near copy of a credited state item. They have not been judged yet: for official sourcing, whether the claim went unchecked or was independent journalism; for a weak signature or a near copy, whether the piece is state text. This is a waiting line, not a verdict, and these articles are never folded into state origin, unchecked state sourcing or independent journalism until they are judged.
official_chinese_sourcing_verification_p.distinction_note: This is easy to confuse with unchecked state sourcing, and the site's own wording makes that worse: one is a completed (if machine-made) judgement that a claim went unchecked, the other is a pile of articles nobody has judged yet. Read 'verification pending' as 'still in the queue' and 'unchecked state sourcing' as 'the model looked, and the claim was not checked.'

independent_journalism.label: Independent journalism
independent_journalism.definition: The outlet's own reporting. This can include quoting Chinese officials, as long as the outlet also confirms, adds context to, or challenges what they said. It also includes reporting an official Chinese position, policy, warning, threat, opinion or denial, with or without outside comment.

not_relevant.label: Not relevant
not_relevant.definition: The article passed the keyword screen, but once its full text was read it does not substantively concern China: China comes up only in passing, or the keyword matched something else. State text never lands here whatever its topic: a Xinhua story about another country, run without substantive change, is state origin. These articles are not a finding on their own; they are kept so that every article read carries a label.

paywalled_unread_and_uncounted.label: Paywalled, unread and uncounted
paywalled_unread_and_uncounted.definition: The article sits behind a paywall the tracker could not get past, so it was never read and never sorted into any of the categories above. It does not count as state origin, unchecked sourcing, independent journalism, or not relevant. It is missing data, not a zero, and a country with a lot of it is not comparable to a country with little of it.

wire_credit.how_it_arrives: The Chinese state outlet's name (Xinhua, CGTN, China Daily, Global Times, People's Daily, China News Service) appears as the story's byline, credit line, or dateline, the same way any wire service is credited when a newspaper runs its copy.
wire_credit.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: a byline reading '(Xinhua)' at the top of a short business story about a new trade route.

distribution_stamp.how_it_arrives: The article carries the markings of a commercial press-release distribution service, the kind any company uses to push out an announcement, alongside the name of a Chinese state entity, showing it arrived as a distributed release rather than as staff reporting.
distribution_stamp.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: a story tagged '(via PR Newswire)' that repeats a Chinese state company's own announcement almost word for word.

sponsored_disclosure.how_it_arrives: The outlet discloses, as it is required to for any advertiser, that the piece is sponsored content or a paid partner placement, and the sponsor is a Chinese state entity.
sponsored_disclosure.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: a page labelled 'Sponsored Content' carrying an upbeat feature about a Chinese province, paid for by a state agency.

diplomatic_byline.how_it_arrives: The piece is signed by a Chinese ambassador, embassy official, or other named Chinese diplomat, usually as an opinion column in a local paper.
diplomatic_byline.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: an opinion piece bylined 'By [Name], Chinese Ambassador to [Country]', published in a newspaper's opinion section.

uncredited_copy.how_it_arrives: State text that another outlet ran with a credit line, republished here without it, judged by the model. The tracker finds the near copy; the model decides whether it is that state text, unaltered.
uncredited_copy.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: a short trade story with no byline or credit, worded almost exactly like an item another paper ran the same day under a '(Xinhua)' credit.

unattributed.how_it_arrives: The model judged from the text alone that it is state text run without substantive change, but named no credit line, stamp, disclosure or diplomat's byline as its evidence, and no near copy of a credited item was found: a release that names the state body issuing it and carries no credit line, for example. These labels rest on the model's call and on nothing a reader can point to on the page, so they are the least certain of the six routes until hand coding checks them; the route list under Methodology gives their current number.
unattributed.illustrative_line: Illustrative only, not a quote from a real article: a short unbylined report on a Chinese provincial trade fair, worded like agency copy, that carries no credit line and names no source.

faq.question: Why is Italy so high?
faq.answer: Most of Italy's count comes from one outlet, Italpress, a national news agency that runs Xinhua copy under a joint credit line, "(XINHUA/ITALPRESS)", which the tracker's rules read as a wire credit. Italy's biggest newswire, ANSA, ran a formal Xinhua Italian-language news service from 2019 to 2022, then ended it. Italy also has more monitored outlets than most countries, so there are more chances for this material to show up. The outlet and the route that carry the most in the current window are counted from the data and shown when you point at Italy on the map.

faq.question: Why is the United States zero?
faq.answer: Where the United States shows zero, none of the US outlets I monitor (the country panel lists them) carried a state-origin article in the window shown. State-origin material does reach American readers, but mostly through global press-release distribution services such as PR Newswire and GlobeNewswire. Those are not national newsrooms; they push the same releases to subscribers in many countries at once, so crediting them to one country would be misleading. The tracker counts them as a stratum of their own, Worldwide distribution, which sits in the ranked list and the country search beside the countries and is drawn nowhere on the map. It is never added to the United States or to any other country's count, and it is part of the world total.

faq.question: Why is China itself excluded?
faq.answer: China is the origin of the content this tracker measures, not a destination for it. Counting Chinese domestic media would mean counting the source as if it were a receiving newsroom. Chinese outlets appear in this project only as senders, as the Xinhua, CGTN or China Daily byline inside another country's coverage, never as a monitored country in their own right.

faq.question: Why is Taiwan zero?
faq.answer: Taiwan's monitored outlets all publish in English: Taipei Times, Focus Taiwan (the English service of the Central News Agency), Radio Taiwan International's English service, DIGITIMES and New Bloom Magazine; the country panel lists the current set. Most of Taiwan's press publishes in Chinese, and the Chinese-language Taiwanese outlets in the registry, among them the Liberty Times, United Daily News and CNA's Chinese service, are excluded, because I do not read Chinese and machine translation would miss the distinctions the coding turns on. Taiwan's zero therefore describes a handful of English-language outlets, not Taiwan's press as a whole.

faq.question: How reliable is the unchecked state sourcing count?
faq.answer: Unchecked state sourcing is judged once by an AI model applying the author's written codebook. Until people check that judgement, the counts are provisional and marked as such wherever they appear. The check is hand coding: the owner and two research assistants code a fixed random sample, about 200 articles in each language with at least 300 model-labelled articles, drawn separately for each language and, within each language, spread across the model's categories so that unchecked state sourcing is well represented. They code blind, without seeing the model's label. The counts are published only if Cohen's kappa between their codes and the model on unchecked state sourcing versus independent journalism is at least 0.6, with the coders and the model each placing at least 10 articles in unchecked state sourcing, overall and in each language with enough items; below that they are withheld, not merely flagged. A separate check has the same model, with the same prompt, re-judge a sample of its own past calls. That shows only whether the judgement is stable, not whether it is correct: a bias the model holds every time would pass it, so such a check never makes counts publishable. The last one ran under an earlier version of the classifier's instructions, so it is kept as history and neither supports nor withholds any count; a new one runs once enough articles are labelled under the current instructions.

faq.question: Does every story that quotes Beijing count as unchecked state sourcing?
faq.answer: No. It counts only when the article's central content is a factual claim from a Chinese official or state source, such as a figure, an account of an event, or who did what, passed on as fact with no independent check. An article that reports what Beijing says it wants, plans, warns, threatens, believes or denies is reporting a stated position, and that is independent journalism even when nobody else is quoted. A report that exports rose 8.7 percent, on the commerce ministry's word alone, counts; a report that the foreign ministry warned Manila it would take resolute measures does not. This rule was added to the model's instructions on 12 October 2026. Model labels made before it are being redone by the model in priority tiers, with unchecked state sourcing and state origin labels among the first and the oldest first within each tier (the methodology file gives the current order), using up to half of each day's model calls; until an article's new label arrives its old one stands, and grey ticks on the timeline mark the days still waiting.

faq.question: Is a computer deciding this?
faq.answer: Not on its own: the method is mine, and the computer carries it out. I decided which outlets to read, the China keyword lists, the credit lines and datelines that mark state text, and a written codebook for the harder cases. Fixed rules decide the cases with a visible marker, such as a Xinhua credit line, with no AI involved. An AI model following my codebook, and shown only the headline and the text, never the outlet or the country, makes the other calls: whether a locally written article checked an official Chinese factual claim or just repeated it, and whether text with no visible marker is state copy. That covers many state origin labels as well as unchecked state sourcing; the methodology file gives the current split. The model's calls are not perfectly repeatable, which is why hand coding of a fixed sample checks them, and the methodology section shows how many articles a person has reviewed so far.

faq.question: How new is the data?
faq.answer: The earliest article in this dataset was discovered on 2026-09-03. Everything here covers the weeks since then, not years of history. Treat any pattern you see as an early read, not an established trend.

faq.question: How often is it updated?
faq.answer: The tracker polls its outlets on an hourly schedule. In practice the interval varies, because the free scheduling service it runs on delays or skips runs when it is busy, so hourly is a target, not a guarantee. Every run's real start and finish time is written to a log.

faq.question: What does stance toward government mean?
faq.answer: It records whether an outlet supports its own country's government, is independent of it, or sides with the opposition, as described by Reporters Without Borders, Freedom House or the Media Ownership Monitor. An outlet's description of itself does not count. Governments change, so each stance carries the year its source describes, and a source older than a change of government is not used. State owned outlets without editorial independence are shown as state controlled.

faq.question: Why are so many outlets "not assessed" for political leaning?
faq.answer: Leaning is only assigned when a specific, named source says so: a Wikipedia media list, Media Bias/Fact Check, a press-freedom group's ownership monitor, or something similar. It is never guessed from an outlet's name, language, or country. Media Bias/Fact Check is based in the United States and rates outlets on a US scale, so where it is the only source for an outlet outside the United States the leaning is kept but shown with a caution, and the note under the chart says how many leanings come from each kind of source. Many of the outlets I monitor, most of them small or local, have no such source behind them, so they are marked not assessed rather than given a guess.

faq.question: Who made this and why?
faq.answer: I did: the tracker's citation line credits me, Daniel Banin. What the tracker can and cannot tell you is in my note at the end of the methodology section.

faq.question: How do I report a mislabelled article?
faq.answer: Open an issue on the project's GitHub page and include the article's link and the category you think is correct.

country_notes.ITA: Most of Italy's state-origin count comes from one outlet, Italpress, a national news agency that runs Xinhua copy under the joint credit line "(XINHUA/ITALPRESS)". Italy's largest newswire, ANSA, ran a formal Xinhua Italian-language news agreement from 2019 until ending it in 2022. Sources: https://www.ansa.it/english/news/general_news/2019/03/22/ansa-xinhua-collaboration-accord-signed_aeba934e-af01-43a2-b5a3-cb90b4852fc4.html, https://decode39.com/3977/italy-media-broke-china-propaganda-ansa-xinhua/
country_notes.IDN: Indonesia's count is carried mainly by the national news agency Antara and its English-language wire Antara English, mostly through the wire-credit route. Antara has run a news-exchange arrangement with Xinhua dating to 1957, expanded in 2025 with fresh cooperation agreements with Xinhua and China Media Group signed during a Chinese premier's state visit. Source: https://en.antaranews.com/news/356517/antara-establishes-cooperation-with-cmg-xinhua
country_notes.MYS: In the data, Malaysia's largest carrier is Utusan Malaysia, mostly through the press-release-stamp and unattributed routes, not the national wire Bernama. Bernama has its own long-running Xinhua news-exchange agreement, first signed in 1985 and renewed several times since, but that pipeline is not what shows up as the top source in this window. Source: https://www.bernama.com/en/news.php?id=2255080
country_notes.LAO: Nearly all of Laos's count comes from a single outlet, The Laotian Times, mostly through disclosed sponsored placements rather than a plain wire credit. Xinhua and the Lao News Agency signed a news-exchange agreement in 2018 covering text, photo, audio and video cooperation. Source: http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2018-10/25/c_137555818.htm
country_notes.ZAF: South Africa's largest carrier is IOL, the website of Independent Media, in which two Chinese state-owned entities, China International Television Corporation and the China-Africa Development Fund, took a 20 percent stake as part of a 2013 financing deal. The route each label arrived by is counted in the country panel. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Online, https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2019-11-13-a-tangled-web-woven-the-pic-and-independent-media/
country_notes.GUY: Guyana's count is almost entirely one outlet, Village Voice News, mostly through the wire-credit route. I could not find a public agreement that explains this pipeline, so this is what the data shows and no more.
country_notes.SGP: Singapore's count is carried mainly by CNA (Channel News Asia). Singapore's Chinese-language press is excluded under the project's language rule, so the figures describe its outlets in other languages. I found no public agreement to cite; this is what the data shows.
country_notes.TCD: Chad's count is carried mainly by one outlet, Alwihda Info, and rests on the model's judgement: the model labelled the articles state origin without a signature the rules can name. I found no public agreement to cite.
country_notes.MLI: Mali's count is carried mainly by Malijet, mostly through the wire-credit route. I found no public agreement to cite; this is what the data shows.
country_notes.BRA: Brazil's small count is led by the business outlet Exame, including disclosed sponsored placements. I found no public agreement to cite.
country_notes.PER: Peru's count is led by La República, mostly through disclosed sponsored placements. I found no public agreement to cite.
country_notes.IRN: Iran's count is small. One of its monitored outlets, Mehr News English, is run by Mehr Media Group, which signed a media-cooperation memorandum of understanding with Xinhua in October 2024; the agreement does not make Mehr the outlet that carries the count, and the carrier shown for Iran is counted from the data. Source: https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/505051/Mehr-Media-Group-signs-MoU-with-Xinhua-News-Agency
country_notes.HKG: Hong Kong is a Chinese special administrative region. Its outlets do not pass the tracker's keyword screen merely for naming their own territory, and a Hong Kong story with no mainland angle counts as China coverage only when it substantively concerns the Chinese state or its policy. Releases and placements of the Hong Kong government and its statutory bodies count as state origin, as the methodology file explains. Hong Kong's Chinese-language outlets are excluded under the project's language rule, so the outlets monitored here publish in English. I found no public agreement to cite.
country_notes.GIN: Guinea's count is small. I found no public agreement that explains it, so the carrier and route shown for it are what the data shows and no more.
country_notes.SEN: Senegal's national news agency, APS, has one of the longest-running of these partnerships, a Xinhua content agreement dating to 1978 and renewed in 2019. APS is not necessarily what carries Senegal's count: the carrier shown for Senegal is counted from the data. Source: http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2019-07/19/c_138240476.htm
country_notes.WLD: Not a country. Worldwide distribution is the press release wires, PR Newswire and GlobeNewswire, whose releases are pushed to subscribers in many countries at once. The releases are counted here as a stratum of their own, never attributed to the United States, where the services are registered, and never added into any country's numbers, which would count each release once per country. There is no territory to draw, so the stratum has no place on the map.

captions.map_timeline_caption: This strip shows the world's daily total for whichever measure and time window you have selected above. Moving it only changes the map; the theme section further down keeps its own separate timeline. Orange bars mark days when more candidate articles were waiting than the model's daily budget could judge, so those days are cut short, not actually quiet. Red ticks mark days when the collector on the owner's machine, which alone collects some outlets, was offline for part of the day. A dashed line marks a change in the classification rules, and grey ticks along the top mark days whose labels were made under older rules or an older version of the model's instructions and are still waiting to be redone; a dotted gold line marks a change in which articles even enter the count in the first place.
captions.notes_strip: A single line above the map that surfaces only what would change how you should read today's numbers right now: for example, a batch of articles still waiting to be judged, a data collector that has gone quiet, or labels still running under an older rule version. Everything it mentions, and more besides, is written out in full under Methodology.
captions.side_panel_labels: Click a country, on the map or in the ranked list, and a panel opens with that country's numbers broken into six rows: state origin, unchecked state sourcing, articles flagged for the model and still waiting to be judged, independent journalism, not about China, and paywalled articles that were never read at all. Below that sit a time chart, a breakdown of how any state-origin material arrived, the list of monitored outlets, and the individual articles behind the count.
captions.ranked_list: Every monitored country, lined up from most to least by whatever measure and window you have chosen. A small triangle, on the map, or an exclamation mark, in this list, next to a country is not a rating of how much state media it has. It flags a data-quality problem specific to that country: for example, a large share of its articles were behind a paywall and never read, a chunk of its feed checks came back empty because items were missed in between, the collector on the owner's machine went offline for part of the window, or it mostly publishes in a language our keyword lists do not cover yet. Open the country to read exactly which warning applies. A warning means the number is less certain, not that the country is worse.
captions.theme_counter_intro: Every article about China is tagged with any theme whose keywords show up in its headline, summary, or body: things like diplomacy, trade, Belt and Road investment, technology, military and security, Taiwan and Hong Kong, human rights, China's domestic politics, culture, and disasters or health. One article can carry several tags, or none, so the tags do not add up to the article count. These are keyword matches, not a person reading each piece, so a striking number here is worth checking against the actual articles before you repeat it.
captions.leaning_chart_note: Every outlet we monitor is sorted by two things, when a cited, named source lets us: its political leaning, judged against its own country's spectrum, and who owns it. State controlled means state owned with no editorial independence. An outlet with no source backing a label is marked not assessed rather than guessed at, so this chart describes the outlets we could check, not the whole registry.
captions.stance_chart_note: In many countries the divide that matters is not left against right but for or against the government. This view groups outlets by how an independent monitor describes them: state controlled, pro-government, independent of both sides, or aligned with the opposition.

findings_template: About {state_share_of_china} of the China-related articles from monitored outlets since {since} came from the Chinese state itself, rather than from a local reporter.
{top_country} carried more than any other country in the last 30 days: {top_country_count} state-origin placements{top_country_items}, {top_country_share} of the world's total{top_carrier_clause}.
Among outlets with a known owner, {ownership_rate_comparison}, counted in placements per outlet.
cta: Download the full daily counts as a CSV from the Methodology section to check any of this yourself, cite the tracker using the citation line at the bottom of that section, or, if you spot an article that looks mislabelled, open an issue on the project's GitHub page (https://github.com/dbanin/china-media-tracker/issues) with the article's link and the category you think is right.
